title: 22. Interview: Prometheus
summary: Interview Q&A for Prometheus — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Prometheus interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Why does Prometheus use a pull model instead of push? What are the trade-offs?
**Answer:** Prometheus pulls metrics by issuing HTTP GET requests to a `/metrics` endpoint on each target, rather than having targets push metrics to it. The pull model has three advantages. First, it is symmetric: Prometheus knows whether a target is alive by whether the scrape succeeds — a missing scrape is itself a strong signal and generates an `up == 0` alert, whereas a push model cannot distinguish "target is dead" from "target is healthy but not pushing." Second, the operator controls sampling rate: one Prometheus can scrape a critical service every 5s and a low-priority service every 60s, without requiring the target to know. Third, the trust boundary is explicit — a misconfigured or hostile client cannot overwhelm the database by pushing too fast, because Prometheus will simply not scrape it faster than configured. The trade-offs are that pull requires Prometheus to reach every target (awkward for short-lived batch jobs, handled via Push Gateway), and that pull across network boundaries requires federation or relays. SoundCloud's original choice of pull was driven by the operational visibility it provided — every target's health is a first-class metric.

**Visual:**
```
Pull:   Prometheus --GET /metrics--> target
        target down? -> up=0 -> alert  (explicit)
        rate controlled by Prometheus

Push:   target --send metric--> TSDB
        target down? -> no signal  (ambiguous)
        rate controlled by client (risk of flood)
```

### Q2. What are the four Prometheus metric types, and when do you use each?
**Answer:** Counter is a monotonically increasing value (resets only on process restart) — use for total counts like `http_requests_total` or `errors_total`; you compute rates with `rate()`. Gauge is a value that goes up and down — use for current-state measurements like `memory_bytes`, `queue_depth`, `temperature`, `in_flight_requests`; you read it directly. Histogram is a distribution of values bucketed into configurable ranges, exposing `<metric>_bucket{le="..."}` counts plus a `_sum` and `_count` — use for latency distributions; you compute quantiles with `histogram_quantile(0.99, ...)`. Summary pre-computes quantiles on the client side, exposing `<metric>{quantile="0.99"}` directly — use only when you cannot aggregate across instances (rare) and never for metrics you will sum across services. The Prometheus team recommends Histogram over Summary for almost all use cases, because Summary's pre-computed quantiles cannot be aggregated correctly — the p99 of two summaries is not the p99 of the combined distribution. Native histograms (Prometheus 2.40+) make bucket boundaries dynamic, removing the last argument for Summary.

**Visual:**
```
Counter   http_requests_total 42         -> rate()[5m]
Gauge     memory_bytes 1.2e9             -> read directly
Histogram http_dur_seconds_bucket{le=0.1} 500  -> histogram_quantile(0.99, ...)
Summary   http_dur_seconds{quantile=0.99} 0.15 -> NOT aggregatable
```

### Q3. What is the cardinality trap, and how do you avoid it in Prometheus?
**Answer:** The cardinality trap is the explosion of time series that occurs when a metric has high-cardinality labels. Every distinct combination of label values creates a new time series, and Prometheus stores each series independently — so a metric with labels `method` (10), `status` (60), `route` (500) creates up to 300,000 series, which is fine, but add a `user_id` label with 260 million values and the database explodes. The TSDB degrades nonlinearly above ~10 million active series per server — memory grows, query latency spikes, and the server eventually OOMs. The cardinality trap is the single most common cause of Prometheus outages in production. The rules to avoid it: never put unbounded labels (user_id, session_id, request_id, trace_id, IP address) on metrics — use logs or traces for those; cap the cardinality of every label (e.g., normalize routes to a fixed set, drop unknown paths); use `label_keep` and `label_drop` relabeling rules to strip high-cardinality labels at scrape time; and monitor the `prometheus_tsdb_head_series` metric to catch cardinality growth before it becomes an outage. A real case: a team adding a `user_id` label to a counter at a 10-million-user service took down their Prometheus in 30 minutes.

**Visual:**
```
Safe labels:    method(10) status(60) route(500)  = 300K series  OK
Explosive:      + user_id(260M)                    = 78B series   OUTAGE

Rule: never label metrics with user_id, session_id, request_id, trace_id, ip
      -> use logs/traces for those
      -> monitor prometheus_tsdb_head_series for growth
```

### Q4. Explain PromQL's instant vector, range vector, and scalar. How do they differ?
**Answer:** An instant vector is a set of time series each with a single value at the latest timestamp — `http_requests_total` returns the most recent value of every series matching the selector, which is what most dashboard charts render. A range vector is a set of time series each with a range of samples over a time window — `http_requests_total[5m]` returns all samples in the last 5 minutes for every matching series; range vectors are not directly plottable but are inputs to functions like `rate()`, `increase()`, and `avg_over_time()`. A scalar is a single numeric value with no labels — `1024` or `2.5e6`; scalars are used in arithmetic with vectors, like `memory_bytes / 1024 / 1024` to convert bytes to megabytes. The fourth type, string, exists for completeness but is rarely used. The mental model is: instant vectors are the leaves of dashboard charts, range vectors are inputs to functions that compute rates or moving averages, and scalars are constants in arithmetic. Understanding the type of each sub-expression is the key to writing PromQL — `rate(http_requests_total[5m])` returns an instant vector (the rate per series), and `sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))` aggregates that into a single-series instant vector.

**Visual:**
```
Instant vector:  http_requests_total               -> {a=1} 42, {b=2} 17
Range vector:    http_requests_total[5m]           -> {a=1} [40,41,42], {b=2} [15,16,17]
Scalar:          1024                              -> 1024

rate(http_requests_total[5m])        -> instant vector (per-series rate)
sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))   -> instant vector (one series, total rate)
memory_bytes / 1024 / 1024           -> instant vector (bytes -> MB)
```

### Q5. What is the difference between a Counter and a Gauge, and why does `rate()` only work on Counters?
**Answer:** A Counter is monotonically increasing — it only goes up (or resets to zero on process restart), so the difference between two samples reflects the number of events between them, and `rate()` computes that difference per second. A Gauge goes up and down — current memory, queue depth, temperature — so the difference between two samples reflects a state change, not an event count, and `rate()` is meaningless on a Gauge (it would report negative rates when the gauge decreases, and the result would not represent any meaningful quantity). The rule: use `rate()` and `increase()` only on Counters; use `avg_over_time()`, `max_over_time()`, and `min_over_time()` on Gauges. The Counter-reset problem is what `rate()` solves: when a process restarts, its counter goes from, say, 1000 to 0, and a naive difference would report -1000 events per second. `rate()` detects the reset (counter goes backward) and treats it as a reset, extrapolating the rate based on the samples before the reset and the samples after. This is why you must use a Counter for any cumulative metric — a Gauge used as a counter will produce wrong rates when it decreases, and Prometheus will not detect the reset.

**Visual:**
```
Counter: 0 -> 100 -> 250 -> 400 -> [reset] -> 0 -> 50
         rate() handles reset, returns ~1.5 events/s throughout

Gauge:   50 -> 30 -> 70 -> 20 -> 60   (memory, queue)
         rate() returns -2, +4, -5, +4 (meaningless)
         use avg_over_time() or max_over_time() instead
```

### Q6. Why is Prometheus not clustered, and how do you achieve high availability and long-term storage?
**Answer:** Prometheus is intentionally single-server — the design team decided that the operational complexity of clustering (consensus, sharding, rebalancing) outweighed the benefit for typical workloads, and that single-instance reliability with WAL replay was high enough. High availability is achieved by running two identical Prometheus instances, both scraping the same targets, both behind a load balancer or with a VIP — if one fails, the other continues to serve queries, with the caveat that the two instances may have slightly different sample timestamps. Long-term storage and cross-instance query are achieved by adding a remote layer: Thanos (sidecar + store + compactor + query) uploads Prometheus blocks to object storage and provides a global query layer; Cortex and Mimir are horizontally-scalable multi-tenant Prometheus-compatible backends that use remote_write to ingest from many Prometheus instances and provide a single query endpoint; VictoriaMetrics is a drop-in replacement with its own clustering. All these systems speak PromQL, so the application's queries and dashboards do not change. The official position is: use single Prometheus up to ~10 million series per server; for higher scale or for long-term storage, add Thanos, Cortex, Mimir, or VictoriaMetrics rather than trying to cluster Prometheus itself.

**Visual:**
```
Single Prometheus:  [scrapes targets] -> local TSDB -> Grafana
                     (good to ~10M series, 15d retention)

HA pair:            [Prom-A] --\
                    [Prom-B] ---+--> Grafana LB
                     (same scrape, slightly diff timestamps)

Long-term + scale:  Prom-1,2,3 --remote_write--> Mimir/Thanos
                    (horizontal, multi-tenant, S3-backed)
                    Grafana queries Mimir (one PromQL endpoint)
```

### Q7. How does Prometheus service discovery work, and why is relabeling needed?
**Answer:** In dynamic environments (Kubernetes, autoscaling cloud VMs), targets appear and disappear constantly, so hardcoding IPs is unworkable. Service discovery integrates Prometheus with the orchestrator's API: `kubernetes_sd_configs` queries the Kubernetes API for pods matching a label selector and rebuilds the target list every few seconds; `ec2_sd_configs`, `gce_sd_configs`, `azure_sd_configs` do the same for cloud VMs; `dns_sd_configs` resolves SRV/A records; `file_sd_configs` reads a JSON/YAML file that an external process updates. Discovered targets come with metadata labels like `__meta_kubernetes_pod_name`, `__meta_kubernetes_namespace`, `__meta_kubernetes_pod_container_port_number` — these are prefixed with `__` and dropped after relabeling. Relabeling rules transform discovered targets: copy a metadata label to a real label (`__address__` to `instance`), drop unwanted labels, add metadata like `environment` or `region` based on the target's tags, map a pod's container port to a scrape path, or drop targets that do not match a pattern (e.g., drop pods without `prometheus.io/scrape: "true"` annotation). The combination of service discovery plus relabeling is what makes Prometheus work in dynamic environments without manual config changes — a new pod is scraped automatically within seconds of being scheduled.

**Visual:**
```
k8s API -> pods matching label app=checkout
           __meta_k8s_pod_name=checkout-abc
           __meta_k8s_pod_ip=10.0.3.5
           __address__=10.0.3.5:8080

relabel rules:
  - source_labels: [__meta_k8s_pod_name]
    target_label: pod
  - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_namespace]
    target_label: namespace
  - action: keep
    source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_scrape]
    regex: "true"

-> Prometheus scrapes 10.0.3.5:8080/metrics with labels
   {pod="checkout-abc", namespace="prod"} within 5s of pod start
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your Prometheus server is using 60 GB of RAM and queries are slow. The TSDB has 8 million active series. How do you diagnose and fix this?
**Answer:** 8 million series is high — Prometheus degrades nonlinearly above ~10 million, so you are close to the cliff. First, identify the high-cardinality metrics: run `topk(10, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"}))` to find the metrics with the most series, then `topk(10, count by (job, instance)({__name__=~".+"}))` to find the chatty jobs. Usually one or two metrics dominate — often a histogram with too many buckets, or a metric with an unbounded label like `user_id`, `session_id`, or `route` (with thousands of routes). Second, fix the source: strip high-cardinality labels in the application code (or use `label_drop` relabeling at scrape), reduce histogram bucket count (5–8 buckets is usually enough; the default 14 is excessive), and normalize routes (group `/users/123` and `/users/456` into `/users/:id`). Third, reduce retention if it is excessive — 15 days is standard; 90 days should be in Thanos or Mimir, not local Prometheus. Fourth, consider sharding: split the Prometheus by team or namespace, so each instance handles 2–3 million series. Fifth, if the workload genuinely requires 8M+ series, migrate to Mimir or Thanos for horizontal scalability. The cardinality audit alone typically reduces series 70–90% without losing signal.

**Visual:**
```
Diagnose:
  topk(10, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"}))   -> chatty metrics
  topk(10, count by (job)({...}))                   -> chatty jobs

Fix:
  1. strip unbounded labels (user_id, route, ip)
  2. reduce histogram buckets (14 -> 6)
  3. normalize routes /users/:id
  4. shorten retention (90d -> 15d local, rest in Thanos)
  5. shard by team or migrate to Mimir
```

### Q2. You need to monitor a Kubernetes job that runs for 2 minutes and exits. Prometheus pull cannot scrape it because it is gone before the next scrape. How do you handle this?
**Answer:** Short-lived batch jobs are the canonical case where Prometheus pull fails — the job may start, run, and exit between two scrape intervals, so Prometheus never sees it. The solution is the Push Gateway, a separate component that batch jobs push their final metrics to at exit, and Prometheus scrapes the Push Gateway on its normal interval. The batch job does `prometheus_push_to_gateway('pushgw:9091', job='my_batch', registry)` at exit, and the Push Gateway holds the metrics (with the job's labels) until they are explicitly deleted or overwritten. The caveats: Push Gateway is for batch jobs only, not for services — services must use the normal pull model. Push Gateway does not expire metrics automatically, so stale metrics accumulate if jobs are renamed or stop running; the team must add a cleanup process. Push Gateway does not deduplicate — if two job instances push with the same labels, the latest overwrites the earlier, which is usually wrong for batch jobs that run in parallel; the team must add an `instance` label distinguishing each run. For very short jobs (under 30 seconds), consider using OpenTelemetry's push model or migrating the metric to a log line that the log pipeline turns into a metric. Real-world: DigitalOcean uses Push Gateway for nightly database backups; CERN uses it for LHC job metrics.

**Visual:**
```
Batch job (2 min life):
  start -> run -> at exit: push metrics to pushgw:9091 -> exit

Prometheus --scrape every 15s--> pushgw:9091/metrics
  (job's metrics live in pushgw until cleaned)

Caveats:
  - pushgw is for batch only, not services
  - metrics don't expire; cleanup script needed
  - parallel jobs need distinct instance labels
```

### Q3. Your team wants to alert when checkout error rate exceeds 1% for 5 minutes. Write the PromQL alerting rule and explain each part.
**Answer:** The alerting rule is:
```
ALERT HighCheckoutErrorRate
  IF sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
     /
     sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout"}[5m]))
     > 0.01
  FOR 5m
  LABELS { severity = "page", team = "checkout" }
  ANNOTATIONS {
    summary = "Checkout error rate > 1% for 5m",
    runbook_url = "https://wiki/runbooks/checkout-high-error-rate"
  }
```
Explanation: `http_requests_total{job="checkout",status=~"5.."}` selects the counter for 5xx responses on the checkout job; `rate(...[5m])` computes the per-second rate over the last 5 minutes, handling counter resets; `sum(...)` aggregates across all instances and routes to get a single total 5xx rate; dividing by `sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout"}[5m]))` (the total request rate, all statuses) gives the error ratio; `> 0.01` fires when the ratio exceeds 1%; `FOR 5m` requires the condition to hold for 5 minutes before firing (filters transient spikes); LABELS route the alert in Alertmanager (severity=page routes to PagerDuty, team=checkout routes to the checkout on-call); ANNOTATIONS give the on-call engineer a summary and a runbook link. The alert is symptom-based (the user saw errors), not cause-based (CPU is high), so it fires when the user is affected regardless of which underlying cause produced the errors.

**Visual:**
```
sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
/
sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout"}[5m]))
> 0.01  FOR 5m

-> page the checkout on-call
-> summary + runbook_url
-> symptom-based (user saw errors), not cause-based
```

### Q4. You need to compute the p99 latency of the checkout service across all instances. Write the PromQL and explain why you cannot use a Summary.
**Answer:** The PromQL is:
```
histogram_quantile(0.99,
  sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="checkout"}[5m])) by (le)
)
```
Explanation: `http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="checkout"}` selects the histogram bucket counters for the checkout job — each bucket is a counter labeled with `le` (less-than-or-equal) giving the upper bound. `rate(...[5m])` computes the per-second rate of each bucket, handling counter resets. `sum(...) by (le)` aggregates across all instances and routes, summing bucket counts per `le` boundary — this is the critical step, because quantiles can only be computed on aggregated bucket counts, not on pre-aggregated quantiles. `histogram_quantile(0.99, ...)` then computes the p99 from the aggregated bucket distribution by linear interpolation between the bucket boundaries that bracket the 99th percentile. The reason you cannot use a Summary: a Summary pre-computes quantiles on the client side (`http_request_duration_seconds{quantile="0.99"}`), but quantiles are not aggregatable — the p99 of instance A and the p99 of instance B do not combine into the p99 of the union. If you averaged two p99s you would get a number with no statistical meaning, and if you took the max you would over-report. Histogram's bucket counts aggregate correctly via summation, which is why the Prometheus team recommends Histogram for any metric you will aggregate across instances.

**Visual:**
```
Summary (wrong for aggregation):
  inst A: {quantile=0.99} 0.15s
  inst B: {quantile=0.99} 0.20s
  avg = 0.175s  <- meaningless, not the p99 of union

Histogram (correct):
  inst A: bucket{le=0.1}=500, {le=0.2}=800, {le=0.5}=1000
  inst B: bucket{le=0.1}=400, {le=0.2}=700, {le=0.5}=900
  sum:    bucket{le=0.1}=900, {le=0.2}=1500, {le=0.5}=1900
  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum) -> correct p99 of union
```

### Q5. You have 20 Kubernetes namespaces, each with its own team. How do you shard Prometheus to avoid one server becoming a bottleneck?
**Answer:** The standard pattern is per-team or per-namespace Prometheus instances, each scraping only its own targets, with a central Thanos or Mimir providing global query. Concretely: deploy one Prometheus per namespace (or per team) using the Prometheus Operator, with `serviceMonitorSelector` matching the team's label so each Prometheus scrapes only its own ServiceMonitors. Each Prometheus stores 15 days locally at full resolution. Each Prometheus runs a Thanos sidecar that uploads completed blocks (every 2 hours) to a shared object storage bucket (S3, GCS). Thanos Store Gateway exposes the object-storage blocks as a queryable source. Thanos Query (or Mimir) federates queries across all the per-team Prometheis and the Store Gateway, deduplicating samples from HA pairs and providing a single PromQL endpoint. Grafana points at Thanos Query for cross-team dashboards and at the local Prometheus for team-specific dashboards (lower latency). The result: each team's Prometheus handles only its own cardinality (typically 1–2M series, well within limits), the central layer handles global queries and long-term storage, and teams retain ownership of their monitoring. This is the architecture used by DigitalOcean, CERN, and most large Kubernetes deployments.

**Visual:**
```
ns=checkout:  Prom-checkout (1.5M series) --sidecar--> S3
ns=payments:  Prom-payments  (2.0M series) --sidecar--> S3
ns=search:    Prom-search    (3.0M series) --sidecar--> S3
                                         |
                                         v
                          Thanos Store + Query (global PromQL)
                                         |
                                         v
                              Grafana (cross-team dashboards)
```

### Q6. Your application exposes metrics on port 8080 at /metrics, but Prometheus reports `up=0` for every target. How do you debug this?
**Answer:** `up=0` means the scrape failed — Prometheus could not get a 200 response with a valid exposition format. Debug in this order. First, check the scrape URL: `kubectl logs prometheus-0 -c prometheus | grep "checkout"` for error messages like "connection refused" or "context deadline exceeded" — these tell you whether the network is the problem or the response is. Second, verify the target is reachable from Prometheus: `kubectl exec -it prometheus-0 -- wget -qO- http://checkout.default.svc:8080/metrics` — if this fails, the issue is DNS, network policy, or the service not being there. Third, check the application is actually serving /metrics: `kubectl exec -it checkout-abc -- wget -qO- localhost:8080/metrics` — if this fails, the app is not instrumented or the metrics endpoint is on a different port/path. Fourth, check the scrape config: `prometheus.tsdb` shows the configured scrape URL — verify `__address__` is `checkout.default.svc:8080` and `__metrics_path__` is `/metrics`. Fifth, check network policies: if the namespace has a default-deny network policy, Prometheus may be unable to reach the target — add an ingress rule allowing Prometheus. Sixth, check the response code: Prometheus logs the HTTP status; a 404 means wrong path, a 500 means the app crashed, a 403 means auth required. Seventh, check TLS: if the app serves HTTPS only and the scrape config does not have `scheme: https`, the scrape will fail.

**Visual:**
```
1. Prom logs -> "connection refused" or "deadline exceeded"
2. Can Prom reach target?  kubectl exec prom -- wget checkout:8080/metrics
3. Does app serve /metrics? kubectl exec checkout -- wget localhost:8080/metrics
4. Scrape config: __address__, __metrics_path__ correct?
5. Network policy allows Prom -> target?
6. HTTP code: 404 (path), 500 (crash), 403 (auth)
7. TLS: scheme=https if app serves HTTPS only
```

### Q7. Your team wants to keep Prometheus metrics for 1 year for capacity planning. Local Prometheus retention is 15 days. How do you architect this?
**Answer:** Local Prometheus is not designed for long-term storage — its local TSDB is optimized for fast recent queries, and retaining a year locally would require tens of terabytes of disk per instance and would slow query and compaction. The standard architecture is Prometheus local for hot data (15 days, full resolution) plus a remote long-term store for cold data (1 year, downsampled). The choices are: Thanos (sidecar uploads blocks to S3/GCS, Store Gateway serves them, Compactor downsamples to 5-minute and 1-hour resolution for queries beyond the local retention), Cortex or Mimir (multi-tenant horizontally-scalable backend that receives `remote_write` from Prometheus and stores blocks in object storage with native downsampling), or VictoriaMetrics (drop-in replacement with built-in long-term storage). For a 1-year horizon, downsampling is essential — at 15-second resolution, 1 year of metrics is ~2 million samples per series; at 5-minute resolution it is ~100K; at 1-hour resolution it is ~9K. Queries for capacity planning typically aggregate over weeks or months, so 1-hour resolution is sufficient and reduces storage 200×. Grafana queries Thanos/Mimir/Cortex with the same PromQL, and the backend transparently picks the right resolution based on the query time range. Real-world: DigitalOcean keeps 15 days at full resolution in local Prometheus and 13 months in Mimir with downsampling.

**Visual:**
```
Prometheus (15d, full res, 15s) --sidecar--> S3
                                            |
                                            v
                          Thanos Compactor (downsample)
                            -> 5min blocks (for 15d-90d queries)
                            -> 1h blocks   (for 90d-1y queries)
                                            |
                                            v
                          Thanos Store + Query (global PromQL)
                                            |
                                            v
                                Grafana (1y capacity dashboards)
```
